question.prompt: On a sheet of paper, Isabella draws a circle of radius \(2,\) a circle of radius \(3,\) and all possible lines simultaneously tangent to both circles. Isabella notices that she has drawn exactly \(k \ge 0\) lines. How many different values of \(k\) are possible?

solutions.explanation:
Let \(O\) be the center of the radius-\(3\) circle, let \(P\) be the center of the radius-\(2\) circle, and put \(d=OP\). Separate the common tangents according to whether the centers lie on the same side or opposite sides of the line.

For a common tangent with both centers on the same side, translate the line perpendicularly \(2\) units toward \(P\). The translated line passes through \(P\) and is at distance \(3-2=1\) from \(O\). It is therefore tangent to an auxiliary circle centered at \(O\) with radius \(1\). This construction is reversible, so it counts these common tangents exactly.

For a common tangent with the centers on opposite sides, the same translation toward \(P\) produces a line through \(P\) at distance \(3+2=5\) from \(O\). These tangents correspond exactly to tangents from \(P\) to an auxiliary circle of radius \(5\).

A point outside a circle has two tangents, corresponding to two reflected right triangles formed by the center, the point, and a tangency point. A point on the circle has one tangent, and a point inside has none. Applying this rule to the two auxiliary circles gives
\[
k=\begin{cases}
0,&0\le d<1,\\
1,&d=1,\\
2,&1<d<5,\\
3,&d=5,\\
4,&d>5.
\end{cases}
\]
Every tangent belongs to exactly one of the two families. Each distance range is possible, so there are \(\boxed{5}\) different values of \(k\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
solutions.title: Translate the common tangents
